utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer? Are you ready for your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. We are ready. As the Trial Chamber knows, this next witness is going to be testifying via video conference link which is being broadcast into the courtroom today from a different location. We are advised that the witness has requested that he be given protective measures of a pseudonym and facial distortion. I'm advised that the technical people are able to give the witness facial distortion even though he's testifying via videolink, and it's my understanding that the pseudonym would be "RR."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any objections for those protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you know that so far we have never objected to these protective measures; however, we are a little bit confused now because the witness -- I don't know. Perhaps we should go into the private session for a moment, lest I be warned once again about his whereabouts, even though we all know where he is staying right now, very far away from here. I believe that this is a country where his safety is ensured, and the very method in which we are communicating with him ensures this. Had he come here, I could understand it perhaps better. But since he's where he is, he's staying where he is, I see no reason for him to have these protective measures, because I think about 95 per cent of witness so far have had some kind of protective measures. Again, we have not objected so far, but perhaps this is going a bit too far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I second -- good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. President. I apologise for not greeting you properly. But I would like to second the -- my colleague Mr. Krsnik's objection, because the witness, first of all, refused to come here, citing as a reason his fear of flying and I don't know what else. So the question that we have is what else is he afraid of? The physical distance between us and him is so large and the distance between where he is now and the place where all these alleged crimes took place is so large, that I see no particular reason for him. Otherwise, we would not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. In this case, the witness might travel to somewhere and there are some people who might live in the surroundings of where he is located. So on the grounds of the precautionary reasons, this Trial Chamber will grant those protective measures asked by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we begin, I could inform the Trial Chamber of what we view to be the relevant parts of the indictment that this testimony would cover. And that would be paragraphs 9 and 11, in the background section of the indictment; paragraphs 15, 16 and 17, which relate to the superior authority of the accused; general allegation in paragraph 21, regarding the widespread and systematic nature of the campaign; paragraph 25, which is part of count 1, which relates to the persecution of the Bosnian Muslim population that was found in Sovici; and also paragraphs 27 and 28 of count 1, which relate to the Heliodrom and other detention centres that the Muslim population was held in; and also paragraph 34 of count 1. The testimony will relate to counts 2 through 5, regarding forced labour on confrontation lines; paragraphs 46 and 50, which are within counts 9 through 12, which relate to torture and beatings of Bosnian Muslims who were prisoners from Sovici; and finally paragraph 53 of count 18, which relates to the forcible transfer of the civilian population of Sovici from that location out to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you prepare a piece of paper which you are going to furnish to Defence counsel and to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe that at the location of the witness, the Registrar Mr. Dubuisson has prepared a slip of paper with the witness's name and the pseudonym, and I believe that we also have one in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just to clarify the procedure, Mr. Dubuisson, the registrar in the third place, is going to show the witness the piece of paper, and he will sign it. And I will show a piece of paper with his name and the pseudonym here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If you push your "Video Evidence" button, I believe that the images will appear that are coming from the remote location.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please stand up. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is going to show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I start, I just want to make sure, because in the courtroom, we are seeing the face of the witness, and I wanted to make sure that the witness's face is not being broadcast outside the courtroom. Okay, and I'm getting an affirmative on that from the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, good morning to you. It's the afternoon here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you hear me well, and can you see me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you, and I can see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before I begin asking you questions, I want to inform you that the Trial Chamber has granted your request for protective measures. And so throughout your testimony this afternoon, I'm going to call you by a pseudonym "Witness RR." Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So I would caution you not to mention your name or to try to avoid saying -- giving information about yourself that would tend to identify you to those of us who are watching here in The Hague. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. It's okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, let me ask you, are you a Bosnian Muslim who was born and raised in the village of Sovici in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were you living in Sovici in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In April of 1992, were you mobilised into the Territorial Defence, or the local TO, for Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in April of 1993, were you a member of the TO for Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In April of 1993, can you tell us, please, who was the commander of the TO in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Dzemal Ovnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to the night of the 16th of April, 1993. Can you tell us, please, what you did on the evening, the night, of 16 April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In the evening, I was at the front line until 12.00, and I went home to sleep until 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. What time did you arrive at the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: When the shelling started, I was at home. And I immediately went to the line, and I was there at about ten past 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know the name of this front-line position where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: It was called Kamen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I believe that in your location, Witness, you should have a photograph which is marked as Exhibit 6.3. And I would ask you to take a look at that photograph at this time, and we can also place it on the ELMO. Now, Witness, are you able to see photograph that's been marked Exhibit 6.3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on that photograph, are you able to see the location or the place that you've called Kamen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. If you have a pen or a marker there, could I ask you to place a circle around the place or the position that you've called Kamen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I circled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Witness, I just wanted to clarify what you said already about the time that you were at Kamen. What time did you arrive at Kamen on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: 8.00 or 8.10 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was that in the evening of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: It was in the morning of the 17th, when the attack started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but we did not see what the witness circled. We cannot see the location which was circled by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could you have it put on before the camera?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Apparently that's being done at this time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you -- Witness RR, you've made the mark. If you have a pen, could you -- okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Here it is, this. I'm circling it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You say you arrived at Kamen on the morning of the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, at ten past 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where were you when the attack actually started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I was at home. I had come back from my shift. I went to bed, and I found myself at home when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And after you then arrived back at Kamen at approximately 8.00 in the morning, what did you do and how long did you remain at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We stayed there until 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you just briefly describe for us, Witness, what happened and what did you observe during the course of that day on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: On the 17th April, I went back home around 8.00. We went to Duga Gruda and Pasje Stijene and Povrsak. I left home and I went to Kamen, to the front-line positions. We held -- we were holding this front line facing the Croatian village so that we would not be attacked from there. And we stayed until 4.00, until Mackovice and Duga Gruda fell. After the fall of Duga Gruda and Mackovice, I started fleeing the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, just to clarify, are Mackovice and Duga Gruda other locations where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, none of the locations have been written down in the transcript. I think we may have problems with the transcript because nothing of the locations, the place names, were entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. Can you make it clear for us? You may ask some questions and ask the witness to spell out those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned two other locations, Mackovice and Duga Gruda. Could you please spell those two places, as best as you know so that we have them spelled correctly in our record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: D-u-g-a, one word, G-r-u-d-a, second word. And M-a-c-k-o-v-i-c-a, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mackovice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now -- and I wanted to ask you again, Mackovice and Duga Gruda, are those other places where other members of the TO also had positions on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: These were members of -- that is the inhabitants of our village that were at Mackovice and Duga Gruda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you were at Kamen and during that day, was any shelling taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know where the shelling was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: It was coming from Risovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what places what positions were being shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Duga Gruda, Pasje Stijene, and Povrsak - that was 8.00 in the morning - and Mackovice. Povrsak, spells P-o-v-r-s-a-k. Pasje Stijene, spells P-a-s-j-a S-t-i-j-e-n-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you remained at this location until about 4.00 in the afternoon. Can you tell us, then, what happened at about 4.00 that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. Around 4.00 in the afternoon, Mr. Tuta called Dzemal Ovnovic telling him that the positions had fallen and that he should come out and surrender and that the soldiers should go to the middle school to surrender, and if they did not surrender, he would continue to shell the village - because the village was shelled since 10.00 - and he was going to start shelling civilians. And Dzemal asked us what to do, and then he went to Obruc, and he said that he would be responsible for the 39 men that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know that it was Tuta who gave this order to surrender or the village would be -- the civilians in the village would be shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Not that they would be shelled but they were already shelled. The shelling started at 10.00. But he would go on shelling the civilians. Dzemal Lulic came, who was sent by Dzemal Ovnovic, the commander, to tell us that Duga Grude and Mackovice had fallen and that there were some prisoners from among our soldiers, and that Mr. Tuta was talking to him, that they were on the line, and that he was -- that the demand came from Tuta that they surrender and that we should go to the middle school, middle -- little school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness, after you and the others on Kamen received this information, tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I decided not to surrender, that I didn't want to go to the school to surrender. I decided to escape the village towards Glavica, together with Dzemal Lulic, with that messenger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then where did you spend, then, the night of the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In the village of Munikoza. That is how far I could get that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the following day, the 18th of April, did you continue to try to move out of the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. I went on towards Jablanica. And on the 18th, I reached the village of Parcani with the rest of the group, those of us who met at Munikoza.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: By this point, on the night of the 18th, how many people were in your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Nine men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were these others -- were these also members of the TO from Sovici who were trying to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the following day, which would have been the 19th of April, did you continue to try to move out of the area toward Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. I had almost reached the village of Orlovac, a Croat village, and that is where I was captured at 4.00 in the afternoon on the 19th -- no, on the 20th, we were captured. It was Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So are you saying, then, that you were captured on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night of the 19th, before you were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Above the village of Orlovac. On the 18th, in Parcani; and on the 19th, we were above Orlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record, I can inform the Trial Chamber the witness does not have the map with him, but I can inform all the parties that the location Orlovac is found on Exhibit 3.3, which is a map that has been received in evidence which was also used during the testimony of Witness Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you say that you were captured on the 20th of April. Could you tell us, please, who captured you and how about -- that came about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We were captured by -- well, Orlovac is a village, and the vantage point is Pomen, something like that. It was three or four HVO soldiers from Doljani - I mean, they were villagers of Doljani - and they captured us -- they captured us there, and a wounded member of the TO, my colleague. So we were captured. They tied up our hands and said they had to turn us over to Tuta. And they took us to Mr. Tuta, and we carried the wounded man in the tent canvas. But they knew there was a wounded man, and so they asked when we got there, "Who is wounded?" And I said this is the one from the Territorial Defence. And this one said, "Well, had I known, I wouldn't have come," because he had come because he did not know the wounded came from the Territorial Defence or the HVO. And then they took us down to the village and turned us over to Tuta's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I'm going to ask that the witness be shown the photograph that's marked Exhibit 8.8. And we could place it on the ELMO here, but I don't know if we're able to get that image as well as the image of the witness at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, looking at Exhibit 8.8, are you able to recognise this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I can, yes. This is the command, that is, where their centre was. That is where we were beaten and battered --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: -- and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before the witness makes any marks with the pen, I'd like to ask, if it's possible, to put the photograph back on the camera for the next couple of questions so that we see the photograph and not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, now, before you make any marks -- and I'm going to ask you to make some marks on this photograph. But before I do that, let me ask you some questions. First of all, can you tell us how you were brought to this place, and give us a description of what you found when you arrived there. Who was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I can. I can answer all of that. We were taken there with our hands tied and our heads down. And several metres, a hundred, 200 metres from the command in this valley, they ordered us to crawl in a single file, and they were hitting us with their boots on the head as we crawled. And we reached the command from the right-hand side. There is a wire and somebody yelling, "Get through. Stand up," so that we go past that wire. And then we were lined up there in front of the command, up to the road, up to the fish pond with our heads down, and then the beating began. Mr. Tuta was standing in front, in front of the soldiers. We were in a circle, and the troops were around us, and that is where we were beaten. And they had taken me to a small house - which is not here - to beat me. And then they said that I should come out and that this gentleman, Fikret Begic, should go in. And then he was taken in, and then he was beaten, and I was taken back to those other eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, let me take you back through this and ask you a couple more questions. You said that there were troops there. Can you give us an approximation how many troops you're talking about that were at this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: There were between 100 and 200 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Many-coloured clothes. There were also some black too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where were those troops -- where were they during the time that you were crawling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Only those four of us who took us -- who captured us were with us, and the rest were in front of the building. I didn't know where they were. When they brought us there, when we had crawled down to the building, it was only then that I spied this large group of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you then were standing next to a structure, a house or a - I'm not sure the exact word you used - where beatings started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: It is. In front of the house, in the parking lot, a large one, in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, now I'm going to ask you to take the pen, and if you can, place a number "1" at the location where you and the others started crawling.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then I'm going to ask you to place a number "2" at the place where you and the others were standing when the beatings began.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I put here "1" and "2."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness, we can see that well from here. Let me ask you: The place that you've marked with the number "2," where the beatings occurred, you've mentioned -- you've mentioned Tuta. Was Tuta present when the beatings were taking place at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. He was in -- he was standing in front of his soldiers. We were in a circle, and then his soldiers were around us, and he was slightly in front of us, in our circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you mentioned that you were taken to a third place that is now not shown on this photograph. Could you tell us -- tell us more about that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We were beaten there, and then I was taken to this small house which is "wattle and daub" which does not exist here, but it was there. It was like a guard post. But I entered, I didn't stay there long, and they immediately told me to get out and that Fikret Begic should go in. And Fikret Begic entered, and they beat him, and I was beaten together with all the rest over there. And so they beat us, and all those others fell down, and only I remained on my feet, and then one of them swore at the balija mother, "Why isn't he down?" And then they battered me so that I fainted. And then I was caught -- and then he caught me by my right shoulder and lifted me but not quite, only so that I would be on my knees, and told me to pick grapes. And I couldn't understand. What grapes? There are no grapes around there. And then one of them was standing and had his arms stretched to the left, to the right, in front of me, to make as if I were picking grapes, although there were no grapes there. But that is only in that position so that he could beat me easier on my stomach and other parts of my body. And then I saw Fikret Begic to my left, lying on his left side, and Mr. Tuta beating him with his pistol on the head and requesting the password to Jablanica. But we had nothing, and he kept beating Fikret Begic on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there for a moment, because I want to ask you some more questions about what you've just said. First of all, could I ask you to take the photograph again and to place a number "3" at the location of this guard house or this place which does not appear any more, at least in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, yes, I put number "3" here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that Fikret Begic was taken into that place after you. Did you see anyone enter that shed or that place with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Why, yes. He entered this guard booth. Soldiers were standing in front of it and told me to come out, and he went in. And I had to keep my head down and move towards those others, and he went in and stayed there behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure we understood what you meant by this "picking the grapes." What was your position, the position of your body, while you were being told to pick the grapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: On my knees. My knees were on the ground, and my feet were on the ground; that is, I was down except that they put me up by my shoulder so that my knees and my feet were on the ground and I was on my -- upright on my knees. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was the position of your arms as you were picking the grapes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, naturally, my hands were outstretched following his arms, because he was raising them. He was turning in front of me and raising them, and raising them to the left, and then I had to stretch to his left, to get at the grapes, which he held in his hands - of course, he had none - and then to the right-hand side. And others were beating me on the stomach and other parts of my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What were they beating you with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Feet, army boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you also said that you saw Begic being struck with a pistol, and I wanted to ask you again, who was doing that? Who was striking Begic with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, at this point I must object to this type of an ID. I have reviewed the statement of this witness quite thoroughly, and in his statement that he gave to the OTP, he says he only saw my client one time and it was a glance. And this Tribunal, I believe in other Chambers, has adopted the fleeting-glance theory adopted from Great Britain, and I object to any identification based on the fleeting-glance doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, first thing I would like to say is that we haven't read that previous statement of this witness. We don't know what happened in this particular moment, and we believe that it's a very essential moment to this case, so we'll allow the Prosecutor to continue with his question. And we don't believe that it will be prejudicial to your client. You may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, my question was: Who was striking Fikret Begic with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Mr. Tuta was striking Fikret Begic with a pistol and asking if we had any contact with Jablanica, if we were maintaining contact with Jablanica. I didn't know who Tuta was. That was the first time I saw him. But I concluded -- that is, I knew that Tuta was attacking us because Dzemal Ovnovic had said that Tuta had called him to surrender, and we were captured. They said that they had to turn us over to Tuta. And then we were taken down there and beaten. And then I saw Tuta best after I had fainted and when they put me up to beat me. So I could not look much around while they beat me because they were beating me too badly. But when they put me up, then I could see, because I had to stretch my arms to pick those grapes. And it happened several times I had to turn right and left; and when I would turn left, I would look to the left, and I could see Fikret lying down and this Mr. Tuta beating him. And I thought, well, that he must be the one because one sees that he is in front of them. He's asking for the contact, and it is -- one can see that he is a kind of a boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, how far away were you from Tuta and Fikret Begic when you saw Begic being hit with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, this is true, 5 or 6 metres. Fikret Begic was lying on his left side facing me, and Tuta was on his knees like I was and striking him, and just face to face, and beating him with this pistol on the head. So Tuta was to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, give us a description of this person Tuta. As you saw him that day, give us the best description that you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I'll describe him to you now. He had glasses, quite thick lenses, a few days' stubble, grey, quite grey. But medium beard, not really long beard; medium, sort of. And I saw him best as he was kneeling for a long time, because I was being beaten and picking those grapes, and I just cast my eyes to the left and to the right, and I saw him kneeling and striking Fikret Begic on his head with a pistol and requesting did we have communication with Jablanica and where had we been heading and what was our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What colour hair did Tuta have on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the hair because I was beaten all that time. I saw as much I could see. So I saw a grey beard, I saw glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: An army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said that he appeared to be a boss. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Because when we were brought there, he stood in our circle in front of us. And then I could only -- because I just cast a look, and I barely noticed him, and the others were standing around us and beating us, that is, in another circle around us and beating us. And then when they took me over there to beat me, but they didn't beat me in that smaller building, and it was then that this major battery started. And then I saw him beat, demanding that contact and questioning. He was the boss. He had even ordered to shoot Fikret Begic and Adis Tasic. And if he could order that, that meant that he was number one. And after all that battery, he ordered that seven of us -- six -- six go to Ljubuski and the seventh would be taken back to the school because it was Denis, underage, and Adis Tasic and Fikret Begic were to be put before the firing squad. And then Blaz, Mr. Blaz from Jablanica, he was a member of his unit, and he saved Fikret and Adis Tasic. He got Adis Tasic by his hair in front of Tuta and said, "Tuta, you should remember that I saved your life." So that means that he's number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I want to make sure that we have the names accurately in the record. Can you give us again the names of the two persons whom Tuta ordered should be executed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I can, sure. I repeat, Fikret Begic, F-i-k-r-e-t B-e-g-i-c, who was beaten in the small house, and Adis Tasic, A-d-i-s T-a-s-i-c. Tuta had ordered them to be put before the firing squad and executed and that the others should be taken to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, you then said that he ordered that you and the others should be taken away. Tell us then what happened at this point. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: And then the -- our names were taken down, and the money that we had, they counted all the money and gave it back to us. They tied our hands once again on our backs with the same rope as before in the woods. And then they put us in a red Niva; that is, they put all eight of us there, except that Blaz saved this Adis Tasic and Fikret, who were to stay there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then did Begic and Tasic come with you and the others in that car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, from this place, this location that's shown in Exhibit 8.8, where were you and the others taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: They loaded us in this red Niva, and there was a car in front and behind us with their soldiers. And then we went to Krcine; that was towards Obruc. We couldn't get out there, and the car could not go up. Then we had to push it. And as we did, I saw the village on fire. I saw the stable of Kukic's house burning, and then we had to again bow our heads. Then we were again put in the Niva, went to Sovicka Vrata. And there, there were troops there. There, they made us come out, and they wanted to chop our arms and legs off and other threats like that. And then after that, we were -- we went on, and we did not stop until Ljubuski any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, since that day, the 20th of April, 1993, have you ever returned to Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again, without giving us information that would identify you, can you tell us, if you know, what happened to other members of your family who were in Sovici on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: They were taken to the school. The military conscripts were taken to Ljubuski, and the older ones and the underaged boys, they left in the school. And the women and children were taken to Krcine. There was somebody who was one of Tuta's soldiers, his name was Junuzovici, and in his house some of these women and children stayed. They slept there for a while, and then the buses arrived sometime at night and they were transferred to Ljubuski -- no, to Gornji Vakuf. We learned that when we came out of the camp and got reunited with our families. Then we were told that they had been transferred to Krcine and from Krcine to Gornji Vakuf, and then on to Prozor to Mount Makljen, and then they were taken off the bus and made to walk towards Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, first of all, how long you remained in Ljubuski and where were you held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We were held in Ljubuski in solitary cells, very narrow, 1.5 metres by 5, and 14 or 15 men slept there in each of the rooms. I was in number 5. It was very hot. We couldn't go to the toilet when we needed to. We had to relieve ourselves in bottles. They took us to perform labour, to unload -- actually, they loaded us on trucks, 100 of us in a truck in a canopied truck, and it was terribly hot under the canopy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Witness, you said that there were 10 to 15 of you, I believe, held in these -- in this cell. Who were those other prisoners? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: There were others. Some were from Stolac, some SDA members who had been taken prisoner earlier, and the ones from the school who were transferred on Sunday, they -- they had surrendered in the Middle Mahala and then they were taken to Ljubuski. On Sunday, the 20th, they were transferred, until then they were in school. And we -- so we found them again in Ljubuski, those who were in Middle Mahala, who were from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was the TO commander, Ovnovic, in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was in cell number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was his condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In very bad condition. He barely survived. Because they beat him in Middle Mahala, and there was an order issued that he be executed, but we found him in Ljubuski. And later on he told us that Prlic had told him that an order had come that he should be executed along with another nine men, that is, the -- that was our group - this is why we were brought there three days later - but that he should not be afraid as long as Prlic was at Ljubuski. But after we were to be taken from Ljubuski, he couldn't guarantee anything for us. And 15 days later, a well-built man came into cell number 6. I had never seen such a man of that build before. He had handcuffs, two pistols --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that last question was simply what was his condition, being Ovnovic. I know this is videolink, and I know we are pressed for time, but I do believe that the answer has become non-responsive. The witness is rambling, and I object to this type of answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, would you please give some guidance to your witness or you may ask some specific questions, since we have certain parts of the answer of this witness already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll do it. He actually has moved to the next thing I was going to ask him, so I thought I would just let him continue, but I can direct the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, let me just take you back. You indicated that there was a group of prisoners who was going to be executed. Was that group executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. I was out in the field. The Red Cross had registered us. Which group? You mean the group of nine that Prlic said was supposed to be executed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple more questions about that. Were there some prisoners there who had been registered by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. We were registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were any prisoners who had been registered by the Red Cross, were any of those prisoners executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, they were executed in Mostar, in Santiceva Street, those that were registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I want to just focus on Ljubuski now, not about Mostar. Was there a group of prisoners that was going to be executed but then was not executed for some reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. It was like this: Several days later, Prlic came to Dzemal Ovnovic and said that he had received an order from Tuta that nine men were to be executed - that is, the eight of us and Dzemal Ovnovic as the ninth - but that he would prevent it while we were under his control, while we were in Ljubuski. But after we were -- we left Ljubuski, he couldn't guarantee for us. But he said that an order had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come, and Prlic said to Dzemal that nine men should have been executed, including him. This is what Dzemal told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross registration have anything to do with the protection that some prisoners received?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that question is speculative in nature. It calls for pure speculation, and I object on that ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may skip this question, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned also earlier that you and others were approached by a large man when you were being held at the Ljubuski prison. And can you please tell us what this person said to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain it all to you in detail. This huge man entered the solitary and asked who had been captured at Doljani. We didn't dare say. And then he recognised Muharem Cilic, because he knew him from Pijesak, and he said, "You were lucky to have been captured only one hour earlier." Why? Because Mr. Cikota, Tuta's deputy, was killed one hour later, and he had ordered that any men that they found be executed. And later on, we learned through the others, after I left the prison, that Denis Skender, when he left when he -- when he left Sovici, that Tuta -- this man from Sovici was killed there. Because when we were captured, they asked who else was there, and we said that there was Salko there, and there was another Salko, but they said, "Well, fuck his mother. You'll be where he went." That was Salko Eglemovic, and he was the one who was actually executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to be clear about what was said by this large man that you've described. First of all, this large man, what was his title or his position? Do you have any idea who he was or what group he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I don't know. He just walked in and later on went to number 5. He beat up Dzemal Ovnovic. He really beat him severely. And then I recognised this Muharem. "And are you from Doljani," he asked him? And he said, "Yes." And he said, "If it had happened a bit later, you would have all been killed because the order had come that you should all be executed," because Cikota was killed an hour earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: And fortunately, we were captured an hour early.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness, how long did you remain detained at the Ljubuski prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then did you go to a different place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: To the Heliodrom in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How long did you remain held at the Heliodrom near Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: The 1st of March, '94, when I was exchanged through the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the conditions that existed in the Heliodrom place where you were held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We were also in large rooms, 70, 80, per room. And we were constantly sent to work to Mostar, to the Santica Street, and different parts of the front line, different locations. And when they lost some of the ground, they would beat us. Ante Buhovac was the worst, and also Miro , among those who were at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you said that when they lost some ground you would be beaten, could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: When the army would take some of their positions, then they would beat us or we would not eat for a day or two. They wouldn't give us anything to eat and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were held 70 to 80 people per room. Can you just give us a description of who the other detainees were? Were they any people that you knew, or were they from other locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: There were men from other places, Stolac, Capljina, and our group, another group from Ljubuski who came about 15 days before us. They were taken from Ljubuski to be exchanged. And when we came to the Heliodrom, we found seven of them in these rooms. We had thought that they had been already exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were there any civilians among the prisoners that you were held with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, there were civilians from our own village. There were underaged boys. Fikret Tasic, for instance, was underage, and he was from our village. And there were some elderly men, 70, 80 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask that you be shown Exhibit 20.10, which is a photograph. Witness, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. The yellow -- three-storey yellow building, that -- this is where we were imprisoned. Where that car is on the first floor is where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, could you take the pen and place a circle around the building that you have just described.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Here, I circled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Witness, you mentioned that during the time you spent at the Heliodrom, you were taken out to work on front line areas. Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how often, how frequently, you and others were taken out to perform labour of this kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: It was not set. It could be 15 days, and then maybe 10 minutes later, I could be taken again. It depended on the unit, who came, and the policeman would just enter from the hallway would point at some men. It didn't matter whether you were working five days straight or not. You never knew when they would come, day or night. They would just take you off to go and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, could you give us or just tell us, if you recall, the different locations where you performed labour and what type of labour, what types of things you had to do on these locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We dug trenches between the lines, and then we sandbagged and fortified the lines. And we placed sandbags in the windows and so on. And my group cleared up the area in Glanica. This was just across from the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the locations you worked in Mostar, in the city of Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I know the bridge near the station, the central station, when you cross over to the right bank, over to the left. It was Tito's bridge, and then right down the street from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Does the name Vinko Martinovic, Stela, mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a suggestive question. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is a suggestive question, Mr. Stringer. You could not ask the name directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. President, the damage has been done already. I don't know how we can undo it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that depends on whether -- what kind of information this witness will provide for us. Let us hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric has the statement, and I think he knows this is not central to either parties' case. It is, nonetheless, relevant, and the question would simply be to the witness if the witness recalls who he worked for, what units he worked for at any time during his detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with this follow-up question, the damage has been increased. That is not at all how this witness testified, so it's not correct at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You might ask some questions about where this witness was working at that time, whether he knows which unit he worked for at that time. You may ask the question like this, but do not directly put the accused's name to it. That's very suggestive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't mean to be suggestive, and I apologise if that's the view. I'll withdraw the question, and I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not fair at all, because the witness never mentioned the name of Vinko Martinovic anywhere in his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, anyway, you have finished your direct examination. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll not pursue this very issue. My suggestion is that we have our break at this moment. We'll resume at 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, cross-examination, please. Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Let me introduce myself. I am counsel for Mr. Mladen Naletilic. I will ask you questions, and I will phrase them in such a way as to get from you the briefest possible answers. Please, because of the videolink, we have some problems, so will you please listen to my question until the end and answer then, so as not to waste time unnecessarily. My first question: When was the TO established in your village? And were you called up, mobilised, or did you volunteer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: It was mobilised in 1992. I was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In my village, in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In other words, a month after the Territorial Defence, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Why, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you then moved over to the BH army, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All Muslims from the village joined the BH army, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In 1992, they were mobilised into the HVO too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who supplied you with weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I don't know. In the beginning, there were only five or six rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But later, in late 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, we were getting some weapons; some we purchased. People managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you all armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how many of you were there in the BH unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: 100 soldiers, 100 conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you also lent a hand by people from Jablanica and other neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Why, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have any heavy armament?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to pause a little before answering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, you may not be familiar with the proceedings before this Tribunal. Since you and the Defence counsel are speaking the same language, please make a pause after you hear the question so that the interpreter could pick up what you are going to say to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness RR, how many statements have you given so far and to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: When I left the camp, I gave it in Jablanica; and then in Sarajevo to this one, to some American lawyer; and this one is the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who was it in Jablanica that you made your statement to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I don't remember. Somebody from the army. I explained, I described all that had happened in Sovici and in the camp. And then to that lawyer in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where is that statement that you made in Jablanica? Do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know where that statement is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I don't. How could I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when you went to Sarajevo, did you have that statement with you when you went to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And it was read out to you by The Hague investigators? You had it with you when they interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment, please. Your Honours, I would like to invite your intervention. This is the second witness - we had the one yesterday, and this one today - they both say that they made their statements to Bosnia-Herzegovinian authorities, that they showed them to The Hague investigators, that they read them like this witness now. We do not have this statement, the one that was made in Jablanica. And I should like to hear from my learned friends, where is that statement; if they have it, to give it to us; if they do not, to explain then why they don't have it, because the witness confirmed today that he had this statement when talking to The Hague investigators and that it was read out to him. In other words, the statement was to be an integral part of his statement and should have been disclosed to us first, rather than hear about it today. We never received that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, would you please shed some light on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, the Bosnian government statements are never an integral part of a statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor. Secondly, we don't have it. We don't -- I don't know why we don't have it. We've looked. I'll ask that we look again. I could be wrong, but it is not among the materials that have been assembled for this witness's testimony. I can't say why we don't have it. All I simply know is that we don't have it. I've never seen it. Every AID or Bosnian government statement that we have was disclosed to the Defence. That's all I can say, Mr. President, at this time. I'll ask that our people do another search, but I can only inform the Trial Chamber and counsel at this time that we don't have any such statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Ole Brondum conducted the interview on behalf of the OTP, I mean with this witness, so he did have that statement. This is the first thing - because this witness has just confirmed it - so this is number one. Number two, it is not true that statements made before the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, notably, the AID, which obviously did all that, that they do not make an integral part of every statement. So far, we have them in 99 percent of the cases. Now, when the witness said that he had it, that he would give it, and The Hague investigators - and we have the name of that investigator - that it was there and now all of a sudden it is not there. The same thing happened yesterday. You will remember that yesterday I also said that we had some procedural problems, but I didn't go into it. The witness also said that he had given a statement, but we did not get it. The Defence, you will understand, would very much like to know what is in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If the Prosecution has not got that statement, there's no obligation for him to disclose that statement. If they have it and they deliberately did not disclose to you, that's another matter. We will make an inquiry into this matter, and I hope I could give you a satisfactory answer on this particular issue. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness RR, do you remember the statement that you gave in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you perhaps have it with you? I mean, amongst the documents that are -- tell me, please, Witness, who proofed you? Who talked to you before today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can just inform counsel that it was our intent to have the OTP witness statement in English, and in B/C/S at the location with the witness. So Mr. Dubuisson should have it, just for your information. It should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much. In that case, I'd like to ask Mr. Dubuisson, if he can hear me, to give the witness the B/C/S version of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And, Witness RR, will you tell me who proofed you for today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Do you need it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, I made a statement in Sarajevo and now here, this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no. My question is: Who prepared you for your today's testimony? Who proofed you for this testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, this lawyer that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you give us his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should go into a private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I can't remember his name. All I know is that he's a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where does he come from, that lawyer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know what word may have been given to the witness in his language for "proofing." I can inform counsel that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, please, Your Honours. This is not rudeness on my part. Your Honours, please, I'm waiting for the witness to answer, and we've been waiting for it for a couple of minutes. I think Mr. Stringer's intervention is merely to help the witness. The witness said very clearly that he was proofed by a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my question is: Where does this lawyer come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Where? Well it was that Mr. Stringer who called me and said that I had to be present to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But a moment ago, you said "my lawyer."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't get your question. It was Stringer. I was with him, and he told me to turn up here at 8.00, that is, at 4.00, to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where did Mr. Stringer talk to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, in Bosnia. Why does it matter where? We met and we prepared this statement that I should attend the trial. Why do you have to know where it was that he prepared me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, I don't, as a matter of fact. Is it where you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, I don't see why I have to say it unless necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, did you go through maps, through photographs? Were you shown photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, maps and photographs, exactly. And I have it all, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you also see Mr. Naletilic's picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I don't have it here right now. I had it in Sarajevo. They asked me if that is the man, and I said yes. But I remember him well. I don't need his picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you now please take this statement and turn to page 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I can do it, yes. It says: "Witness Statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's right. And will you look at the last sentence, the very last sentence. It says: "Prior to the conflict with Croats, we were all armed, mostly rifles, but also howitzers, 82 millimetre calibre. We had two howitzers on our" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, yes, it says: "Howitzers, 82." Well, no. That's what it says. No, that's a mistake. There aren't howitzers, 82. It's 62, mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, let's go through it slowly. Tell me, did you say that to the investigators or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But these are not howitzers. These are mortars, small, short. They are not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which means that you did have heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Why, this is not heavy armament. That is not a large-calibre weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean howitzers is not of a large calibre, or mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Mortars. It says here "howitzers," but it's a mistake. It wasn't howitzers. It was mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, who did you defend against in 1992 and early 1993? Who threatened you as the BH army in that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We were holding the positions against the Serbs, just in case if something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness RR, will you please wait for me to finish my question because of the interpreters. You immediately respond, and then we overlap, and then the interpreters cannot follow. Thank you. Please be patient. Wait for me to finish my question. So let me come to the end of my question. In your last sentence you said, "Allegedly from Serbs."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why allegedly? Were Serbs a menace at the time? Did they threaten you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, we were mobilised by the HVO and the BH army to hold positions in case of an assault by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, what was the strategic relevance of your village for an assault there to take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Because Kupres is there, and that is the Serb zone. That is why we were mobilised. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to tell this Chamber how far is Kupres from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Rather far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, what were your contacts? Who was your superior, I mean, in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Dzemal Ovnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Ernest Kovacevic in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: He was the commander of what? I mean this large gentleman Ernest Kovacevic that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Ernest Kovacevic? Well, of the 1st and the 2nd, and the 3rd and 4th battalions. The commander of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you were which battalion of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion, Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you trained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: No, I had no training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does the nickname Kulje ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Kulje? Oh, Kulje, that's a commander. He was something in the command in Jablanica. The command -- commander of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why didn't he come to Sovici to train you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And does the name Rasim Pilav ring any bell with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Rasim what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Pilav?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Oh, Pilav. No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about Mustafa Cobanov?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: These are people whom I met later on when I left the camp, just ordinary people from the municipality of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Didn't they train you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Nobody trained us. Let us resolve it once and for all and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who brought food to you whilst you were on the positions? Whilst you were in the army, who brought the weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Food, we brought from home. Just take it from home and take it to the line. And once the shift is over, you go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean that as a member of the BH army, an organised brigade in which you were the 4th Battalion, and that you had no logistics whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: We had small logistics for the shifts, just the rudimentary things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who brought you the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: The ammunition was -- was in the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where were the depots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Well, something was at Dzemal Ovnovic's, a small storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where else? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I do not know if there was anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, please, would any rounds of fire be -- rounds be fired at night when one would go through Sovici or Doljani, '93 from January onward?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I was going to ask if counsel could give us the time frame. I wasn't sure if we were talking about 1992 still, but he did that at the very end of his question. So I think I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague is just advising me that he will have no questions, so in order to manage the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In 1993, let's say from January onward, there were no frictions between Muslims and Croats? There were no night shootings, the bombings, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Not so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What do you mean "not so much"? Was there a little, or were there any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: No, there wasn't anything. Only if there was somebody's birthday or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean if there was some kind of celebration, somebody's birthday or somebody's wedding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Again, I have to advise you, Witness - and it may be my mistake, too - please wait until I'm finished with your -- with my question. It is difficult for everybody else to follow. We speak the same language. Croats were able to freely move about the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, they had free movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, this position at Kamen that you held, was that not directly above Croat homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: That position was not held. It was held on the 15th April, when the attack on Jablanica started. Then the Croats went to Middle Mahala, and we had to establish a position facing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where was your command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: The command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In Himza Begic's house, in Begic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is that the hamlet of Begici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You see, we had a witness here - I'm not allowed to give you the name now - who said that the main headquarters was at the Kamen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So it is not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: The correct answer is that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will just ask you to repeat for the transcript, for the record, the Begic houses. In other words, where was the command post? Where was the headquarters? Just repeat it, what you just said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: It was Himza Begic's house in the hamlet of Begici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this is where your commander was staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: That is where we changed shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell me, who was his deputy? Who was his logistics assistant, assistant for security and so on? Because you were in a battalion, after all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Hama Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And for the logistics and security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have radio communication with Jablanica at the headquarters with your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. There was an RUP-12 system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when you were at the positions, you had the Motorolas so that you could communicate with your command post in the village; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes, hand-held Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you were able to communicate non-stop; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, because we don't have any maps, can you tell us, as accurately as possible, what were the positions held by the ABiH? Let's say first outside the village. And please list them very slowly because even the ones you had mentioned previously were not entered into the record. So let's go very slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Mackovice, Duga Gruda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Just take it easy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: In other words, Mackovice, Duga Gruda, Pasje Stijene, and Povrsak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: There was nothing in the village. Just the night watches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You have your statement in front of you. I can see it on the monitor. Will you please go to paragraph 4 from the bottom. The last sentence, you say: "We agreed that the Croats would hold the position in their part of the village and we would do it in our own." So you did have lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: No. These were just patrols. These were night patrols, three-men patrols, that made rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, can I ask what's the relevance for those questions? You have spent 35 minutes, but we are still to come to the central issues of your cross-examination. Are you disputing that the witness was not here -- was not there on that day? If there is no dispute, could we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are a lot of things in dispute with this witness. And we have already heard a number of witnesses. So let's hear them out, and we will obviously analyse their statements. We are already working on it. And it is not possible that there are so many discrepancies. They all lived in the same village, and as far as this witness is concerned, he can hear me, but there are a lot of things in dispute regarding this witness, and we are going to dispute many things about his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, I think the witness can hear what we are saying, and I don't think it's appropriate for counsel to make statements regarding his views of the credibility or the reliability of the testimony of a witness while the witness is in the course of testifying. If he wants to make that argument, there is another time and another place to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we hope you could get over this part of the cross-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me about the positions that you just enumerated, above the village? Did that make the village surrounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: Yes. It was surrounded by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, the watches in the village, you had your own and the Croats had their own, or were they mixed? I'd just like to finish with the distinction between the watches and the lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
utterances.text: At night, we had it in our part of the village and they had it in theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well, you see, thank you. Now, tell me, please, when did the attack start? What was the date? According to you, when do you say the attack started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RR
